Surah 91: Ash-Shams (The Sun)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, its light, when it rises and its dominion becomes full.
And the moon when it follows it (﴿والقَمَرِ إذا تَلاها﴾): it follows it in light and brightness, and that is in the first half of the month, when the moon succeeds the sun in giving light.

﴿By the day when it reveals it﴾: he revealed the sun and made it manifest to observers. This happens when the day has swelled and spread out, because the sun becomes fully manifest at that time. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the darkness, or to the world, or to the earth, even though no mention of them has preceded, as in His saying: ﴿He left upon its back no creature﴾ [Fatir: 45].

Translation:

﴿By the night when it covers﴾: it conceals the sun, and the horizons grow dark. The first "wa" (waw) in such expressions is, by agreement, a waw of oath (qasam). The second is likewise a waw of oath according to some scholars, but according to al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi), the second is a waw of conjunction (atf), because it is not permissible to introduce an oath upon an oath before the first is complete. Do you not see that if you put in its place the particle fa (فاء) or thumma (ثم), the meaning would remain as it is? Those two are particles of conjunction, so the waw is likewise. As for the one who says it is a waw of oath, he argues that if it were a waw of conjunction, it would be conjunction over two governing elements, because his saying "wal-layli" (واللَيْلِ), for example, is governed in the genitive by the waw of oath, and "idha yaghsha" (إذا يَغْشى) is governed in the accusative by the implied verb which is "uqsimu" (أُقْسِمُ). So if you made the waw in "wal-nahari idha tajalla" a waw of conjunction, then "al-nahari" would be conjoined to "al-layli" in the genitive, and "idha tajalla" would be conjoined to "idha yaghsha" in the accusative, and it would be like your saying: "Inna fi al-dari zaydan, wal-hujrati amran" ("Indeed in the house is Zayd, and in the room is Amr"). It is answered that the waw of oath has taken the place of the preposition (ba') and the verb, so that it is not permissible to make the verb explicit with it, and it thus becomes as though it were the element governing both accusative and genitive, and it became like a single governing element which has two effects. Every governing element that has two effects may, by agreement, be conjoined to both of its objects with a single conjunction, as in: "Daraba Zaydun Amran, wa Bakrun Khalidan" ("Zayd struck Amr, and Bakr struck Khalid"), where you raise with the waw and put in the accusative, because it stands in the place of "daraba," which is its governing element. The same applies here.

"And" (wa) and "ma" are here a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya) in ﴿By the sky and He Who built it﴿ ... ﴿and the earth and He Who spread it out﴾ ﴿and a soul and He Who proportioned it﴾, meaning: and by its building, and its spreading out (ṭaḥw), that is its expansion, and the proportioning of its creation in the best form. This is the view of some, but it is not the preferred one, because of His saying ﴿then inspired it﴾, since it causes a defect in the structure of the discourse. The preferred reading is that ma is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and it was chosen over man (who) because of the intended sense of description (waṣfiyya). It is as if it were said: "By the sky and the Mighty Capable One who built it, and by a soul and the Wise One of overwhelming wisdom who proportioned it." The soul is indefinite (nakira) because it refers to a particular soul among souls, namely the soul of Adam, as if he had said: "and one of the souls." Or it refers to every soul, and the indefiniteness is for magnification (taktheer), as in ﴿a soul has known﴾.

Surah 91, verse 8: "So He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness." (Nasafi) He made it aware of its obedience and its disobedience, meaning: He made it understand that one of them is good and the other is ugly.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 91, verse 9:

﴿Indeed he has succeeded﴾ is the response to the oath (jawab al-qasam). The implied wording is: "Indeed, he has succeeded." Al-Zajjaj said: the length of the speech has become a substitute for the lam (of emphasis). It has also been said that the response is omitted, and this is the more apparent view. Its estimated wording is: "Allah will surely destroy them (layudamdimanna Allahu 'alayhim)," that is, upon the people of Makkah, because of their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as He destroyed Thamud, because they denied Salih.

As for "Indeed he has succeeded," it is a statement that follows His saying "So He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness," by way of digression (istitrad), and it has nothing to do with the response to the oath.

﴿He who purifies it﴾: Allah purified it, reformed it, and made it pure (zakiyah).

Surah 91, verse 10:

(p-649) ﴿And indeed he fails who corrupts it﴾: Allah misguides it. ʿIkrimah said: "The soul is successful that Allah purifies it, and the soul fails that Allah misguides." It is also permissible that the corrupting (tadsiyah) and the purifying (tat-hir) are the act of the servant. And "al-tadsiyah" (corrupting, concealing) means diminishing and concealing through immorality. The original form of "dassa" is "dassasa," and the yāʾ is a substitution for the repeated sīn.

Thamud denied [their messenger] in their rebellion (﴿كَذَّبَتْ ثَمُودُ بِطَغْواها﴾). "Bi-taghwaha" means "bi-tughyanihim" (in their transgression), since what drove them to denial was their transgression.

When the most wretched of them set off, (إذِ انْبَعَثَ) — at the time he set about hamstringing the she-camel.

(أشْقاها) — the most wretched of Thamud, Qidar ibn Salif. He was red-haired, blue-eyed, and short in stature. "Idh" (إذْ, "when") is in the accusative case, governed either by "kadhdhabat" (كَذَّبَتْ, "she denied") or by "al-taghwa" (الطَغْوى, "the transgression").

﴿So the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾: Salih (peace be upon him),

﴿the she-camel of Allah﴾: it is in the accusative (nuṣiba) by way of tahdhir (warning), meaning: "Beware of hamstringing her,"

﴿and her drink﴾: like your saying "الأسدَ والأسدَ" (al-asada wal-asada, "the lion, and the lion"), where the second noun is governed by the same warning as the first.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 91, verse 14:

﴿So they denied him﴾, regarding what he had warned them of, namely the descent of punishment if they did it.

﴿Then they hamstrung her﴾, i.e., the she-camel. He attributed the action to them, even though the one who hamstrung her was only one man, like His saying: ﴿Then they called their companion, and he took (the sword) and hamstrung her﴾ [al-Qamar: 29], because they were pleased with him [doing it].

﴿So their Lord leveled over them﴾, He destroyed them with a destruction that uprooted them completely.

﴿for their sin﴾, because of their sin, which was their denying the Messenger and their hamstringing the she-camel.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 91, verse 15:

﴿And He does not fear its consequence.﴾ That is, Allah does not fear the consequence of this deed. In other words, He did that without fearing that anyone would hold Him to account, as a king who punishes fears someone's retribution, because He acted within His own dominion and His own possession.

﴿He cannot be questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23]. "فَلا يَخافُ" (so He does not fear) is the reading of Madani and Shami.
